title: Non-Stimulant ADHD Meds: How They Work
summary: Non-stimulant ADHD meds work over weeks, not hours, and none are controlled substances. See how each class works and when a provider may recommend them.
body_markdown:
Non-stimulant ADHD medications treat ADHD without using stimulants or controlled substances. These medications typically take several weeks to reach full effect. Each non-stimulant class medication works through a different mechanism, and each one may suit patients differently


About[15.5 million U.S. adults had a current ADHD diagnosis in late 2023](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/wr/mm7340a1.htm) . Among adults taking a stimulant,[71.5% had trouble filling a prescription](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/wr/mm7340a1.htm) because the medication just wasn’t available.


At Circle Medical, we offer[ADHD care with a board-certified provider](https://www.circlemedical.com/what-we-treat/adhd) over video and in person. That includes the follow-up visits that being prescribed this type of medications require.


## Non-stimulant ADHD meds: key facts


-


**The five options:** Atomoxetine, viloxazine, guanfacine, clonidine, and off-label bupropion


-


**Controlled substance status:** None of these are controlled substances


-


**Time to full effect:** Several weeks, not the same day


-


**Required monitoring:** Blood pressure and heart rate at the start, after any dose change, and periodically after that


-


**Who prescribes them:** A primary care provider can evaluate, prescribe and monitor them


## What non-stimulant ADHD medications do


Non-stimulant ADHD medications can reduce ADHD symptoms through a different brain pathway compared to stimulants. None of them are controlled substances. No federal scheduling applies.[The FDA has approved four of them for ADHD.](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/treating-and-dealing-adhd) A fifth option, bupropion and certain other antidepressants, is used off-label.


What they are What they aren’t


Prescription medications that reduce ADHD symptoms through non-stimulant mechanisms Controlled substances. None of them carry federal scheduling


Medications that build effect gradually over weeks Fast-acting. You won’t feel one within an hour or two of a dose


Options a primary care provider can prescribe and monitor Restricted to a referral elsewhere before you can start


Treatments that require blood pressure and heart rate checks Monitoring-free. Every label in this category asks for those readings


These medications build their effect gradually over weeks. You won’t feel a change within an hour or two of a dose.


You can start non-stimulant ADHD medications through a primary care provider without a separate referral. But it’s important to have your blood pressure and heart rate checked throughout your treatment. Every medication in this category asks for those readings.


## Six reasons a provider considers non-stimulant ADHD medication for adults


Your provider might suggest a non-stimulant ADHD medication for adults for six reasons:


-


**Side effects you’ve already had.** If you’ve experienced appetite loss, disrupted sleep, or jitteriness on a stimulant, that tells your provider a lot about your drug tolerability. Those effects may be less likely with a non-stimulant medication.


-


**Your cardiovascular history.** Having an elevated blood pressure or a heart condition can change what medication is most appropriate for you. It also shapes which non-stimulant medication your provider would pick.


-


**Co-occurring anxiety.** Some patients find that stimulants sharpen their anxiety symptoms, and a provider will weigh that alongside your ADHD symptoms.


-


**A history of substance use.** Non-stimulants carry no federal scheduling, which can make this a better fit for adults who struggle with substance use.


-


**Supply problems.** If you can’t fill your prescription at a pharmacy, you’re not getting access to medication that can help you. A provider will factor that in when assigning your medication.


-


**Your stated preference.** Some patients would rather not take a controlled substance. That’s a completely valid reason, so if this is your personal preference, it’s best to state it out loud to your provider.


## Three medication classes that treat ADHD without stimulants


Three medication classes treat ADHD without stimulants: norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, alpha-2 adrenergic agonists, and antidepressants used off-label.


None of the three is a controlled substance. Each reaches ADHD symptoms through a different route, which is why they suit different patients.


Class How it works Time to full effect Controlled substance Typical monitoring


Norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (atomoxetine, viloxazine) Slow the reabsorption of norepinephrine, a chemical messenger involved in attention Several weeks No Blood pressure and heart rate at baseline, after dose increases, and periodically. Mood check-ins


Alpha-2 adrenergic agonists (guanfacine, clonidine) Act on alpha-2 receptors in the brain that also help regulate blood pressure Several weeks, with gradual dose increases No Blood pressure and heart rate at baseline, after dose increases, and periodically. Taper when stopping


Antidepressants used off-label (bupropion and others) Affect norepinephrine and dopamine signaling, though the ADHD evidence base is smaller Several weeks No Mood and blood pressure check-ins. Off-label use calls for closer follow-up


[Atomoxetine](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2022/021411s050lbl.pdf) and[viloxazine](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2022/211964s003lbl.pdf) are the two norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors approved for ADHD, and neither is a stimulant. Both slow the reabsorption of norepinephrine, leaving more of it available in the parts of the brain involved in attention and impulse control.


Both labels carry a boxed warning about suicidal thoughts and behavior, and both call for heart rate and blood pressure monitoring throughout treatment. Ask your provider what that follow-up schedule will look like for you.


### Alpha-2 agonists work through a blood pressure mechanism


[Guanfacine](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2019/022037s018lbl.pdf) and[clonidine](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2020/022331s021lbl.pdf) were both originally blood pressure medicine, and the extended-release versions were later approved for ADHD. They act on alpha-2 receptors in the prefrontal cortex, the region involved in focus and impulse regulation. That is a completely different route from stimulants.


Because these medications were originally created for blood pressure issues, you’ll need regular monitoring on these meds. The guanfacine and clonidine extended-release labels both warn about dose-related drops in blood pressure and heart rate. Both also warn against stopping the medication abruptly, since that can cause rebound in high blood pressure.


[Both extended-release products are FDA-approved for ADHD in patients aged 6 to 17](https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.focus.20200032) . Adult use is off-label.


### Bupropion and other off-label antidepressants


An off-label medication means your provider prescribes an FDA-approved medication for a condition outside its approved labeling. The practice is legal and common across medicine, and the off-label use of that medication is based on published evidence even if the FDA has not reviewed that specific use.


Bupropion is the most-discussed off-label option for ADHD. An off-label option can be a legitimate treatment to try, but it cannot promise guaranteed results.


When a provider suggests an off-label medication for your condition, make sure to ask what signs to look for to know that the medication isn’t working.


### Which of the three classes carry FDA approval for adults


Medication Class FDA-approved for ADHD in Controlled substance


Atomoxetine Norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor Adults and children 6 and older No


Viloxazine Norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor Adults and children 6 and older No


Guanfacine (extended-release) Alpha-2 agonist Children and teens 6 to 17. Adult use is off-label No


Clonidine (extended-release) Alpha-2 agonist Children and teens 6 to 17. Adult use is off-label No


Bupropion Antidepressant Not approved for ADHD. Use for ADHD is off-label No


If you’re weighing these against each other, a provider can discuss which one fits your health history. You can[talk to a Circle Medical provider today](https://www.circlemedical.com/what-we-treat/adhd) about your symptoms and treatment options.


## Non-stimulant ADHD medication takes weeks to work


Non-stimulant ADHD medication typically takes several weeks to reach full effect, and often six to eight weeks before you can fairly judge it. An expensive mistake most people make is judging their medication after ten days, deciding it did nothing, and stopping before the medication could make a difference.


On the other hand, the effect of stimulant medication can be felt within the same day, so it’s understandable why you may expect more from your non-stimulant medication. FDA labeling for atomoxetine includes a multi-week wait into the dose adjustment process. Improvement on non-stimulant medication tends to come in a gradual change.


Because the timeline for non-stimulant ADHD medication is longer, we recommend 5 habits for patients choosing this medication category:


-


Put a review date on your calendar before your first dose. Six to eight weeks out. Judging the medication before that date usually tells you nothing.


-


Pick two specific things to track. “Finished tasks I started” is more specific than “felt better.” A vague measure gives you a vague answer at week eight.


-


Get a baseline blood pressure and heart rate reading. Every label in this category asks for one.


-


Note side effects with dates. Early side effects often settle down, and the dates help your provider tell which ones did.


-


Keep the follow-up appointment even if nothing has changed. No change at week three is expected. Use the visit to ask what the next option would be.


However, a few serious symptoms shouldn’t be ignored. If you experience fainting, chest pain, a very slow or racing heartbeat, yellowing of your skin or eyes, or severe abdominal pain, contact a provider or call 911 immediately.


## How non-stimulant ADHD meds compare to stimulants


Non-stimulants and stimulants differ on five things that affect daily life. Those include the speed of onset, federal scheduling, the effect size that the medication trials show, the monitoring required, and exposure to shortages.


Stimulants win on effect size, and any honest comparison will say so.


Non-stimulant medications Stimulant class


**Time to noticeable effect** Weeks Usually the same day


**Controlled substance** No Yes, the main class is federally scheduled


**Effect size, adults, clinician-rated** Around -0.51 for atomoxetine Around -0.61


**Ongoing monitoring** Blood pressure and heart rate Blood pressure, heart rate and scheduling requirements


**Affected by supply shortages** Generally no Yes, reported by most adults taking one


It’s important to note that the average result across thousands of participants in a study won’t predict your result on a non-stimulant ADHD medication. Consider the other factors as well.


Non-stimulants also offer all-day coverage without a wearing-off period.


ADHD treatment plans can also combine these approaches, along with behavioral therapy.


## Common questions about non-stimulant ADHD meds


### Do non-stimulant ADHD meds really work?


Yes, though the evidence is stronger for some than for others. The 2025 Lancet Psychiatry network meta-analysis found atomoxetine reduced core ADHD symptoms in adults at around 12 weeks on both patient-rated and clinician-rated scales. Bupropion has a smaller evidence base rated low quality by Cochrane reviewers. Response varies between people, so a provider can assess whether an option is reasonable for you.


### How long do non-stimulants take to work?


Several weeks, in most cases. FDA labeling for atomoxetine builds a multi-week wait into the dose adjustment process, and the adult trials that established its effectiveness ran for 10 weeks. Alpha-2 agonists are also increased gradually. Plan on giving a non-stimulant six to eight weeks before you judge it, and keep your follow-up appointment even if you notice nothing at first.


### Are non-stimulant ADHD medications controlled substances?


No. Atomoxetine, viloxazine, guanfacine, clonidine and bupropion carry no federal scheduling. FDA labeling for atomoxetine states directly that it “is not a controlled substance.” The guanfacine extended-release label says it “is not a controlled substance and has no known potential for abuse or dependence.” That status puts these medications outside the pharmacy and refill rules that apply to scheduled stimulants.


### Can you take a non-stimulant and a stimulant together?


Sometimes. Both guanfacine and clonidine extended-release carry FDA approval as adjunctive therapy to stimulant medications. That means they are added alongside a stimulant. Combination approaches are prescribed and monitored case by case. They aren’t right for everyone. A provider can discuss whether combining medications is appropriate for you and what monitoring it would require.


### What is the best non-stimulant ADHD medication?


No single non-stimulant is best for everyone. Atomoxetine and viloxazine carry FDA approval for adults, so they’re often discussed first for adult ADHD. Guanfacine and clonidine are approved for ages 6 to 17, which makes adult use off-label. Bupropion is off-label for ADHD at any age. Your health history, blood pressure, other prescriptions and past medication experience shape which one a provider would consider.


### Can a primary care provider prescribe ADHD medication?


Yes. Primary care providers evaluate ADHD, prescribe medication where clinically appropriate, and handle the ongoing monitoring these medications require. Non-stimulants suit that setting well, since blood pressure and heart rate checks are routine primary care work. Circle Medical has 300+ board-certified providers across 32 states, and you can check insurance plans we accept before you book.


## Start an ADHD medication conversation with a provider


Starting the conversation about your ADHD medication should be straightforward. Tell your provider the primary reason why you prefer non-stimulant ADHD medication, or name the things you want your current stimulant ADHD medication to change. Then ask how the new non-stimulant medication is expected to respond within the next eight weeks.


If ADHD symptoms are affecting your work, your relationships or your sleep, speaking with a primary care provider can help. Seek immediate care if you experience fainting, chest pain, an irregular heartbeat, or thoughts of harming yourself while taking any ADHD medication.
